title: Lending, Borrowing, and Interest Rate Curves
objectives: Read a money market from one number: utilisation = borrows / deposits
Understand the kinked rate curve that Aave and Kamino use
Turn a borrow APR into the supply APY a depositor actually earns
See why rates explode during a liquidity crunch

steps.title: How Decentralized Money Markets Work
steps.body:
A DeFi money market is a vending machine that never sleeps and never checks your credit. No loan officer, no paperwork, no handshake — just a contract and one shared pile of tokens.

The roles, before you deposit a single dollar:

- **Depositors are the suppliers.** You lend tokens into the pool and earn interest paid by everyone who borrows from it.
- **Borrowers are the demand.** They overcollateralize — lock $1.50 of SOL to borrow $1.00 of USDC, say — which is what protects your deposit.
- **Nobody negotiates.** The rate is not decided by a committee. It is computed continuously from one number: <Term id="utilisation">utilisation</Term>.

Utilisation is the thermostat of the entire market. Turn it up and borrowing gets expensive while lending pays more. Turn it down and the reverse happens. Almost everything else in this lesson is a consequence of that single dial.

steps.title: The 80% Kink: Why Rates Explode
steps.body:
Utilisation is `U = Total Borrows / Total Deposits`. Deposit $100 and borrow $80, and utilisation is 80%.

Here is the catch that makes money markets clever. At 100% utilisation there would be nothing left for depositors to withdraw. To prevent that quiet bank run before it starts, protocols build a **piecewise kinked rate curve** — a gentle slope, then a cliff.

- **Below the kink (under ~80%).** Rates climb in a lazy line. Borrowing is cheap, think 2% to 8% <Term id="apr">APR</Term>, so people borrow happily and depositors earn a modest yield.
- **At the kink (~80%).** The slope snaps sharply upward. That is the warning line built into the maths.
- **Above the kink.** Borrow rates rocket toward 50% to 80%+, punishing anyone still borrowing while making a fresh deposit wildly attractive.

The market self-corrects with no manager in sight. Demand pushes utilisation past the kink, new deposits are rewarded with a huge <Term id="apy">APY</Term>, and borrowers are squeezed to repay. Liquidity floods back long before the <Term id="liquidity_pool">pool</Term> can be drained dry. The curve *is* the safety mechanism.

steps.title: Under the Hood: The Kink Interest Rate Equation
steps.body:
Every borrow rate in a money market comes from the same two-slope formula, expressed as <Term id="apr">APR</Term>, where `U_optimal` is the kink (often 80%).

`If U ≤ U_optimal:  R_borrow = BaseRate + (U / U_optimal) × Slope1`

`If U > U_optimal:  R_borrow = BaseRate + Slope1 + ((U - U_optimal) / (1 - U_optimal)) × Slope2`

Reading it like a market maker:

- `BaseRate` is the floor borrowers pay even at near-zero utilisation, so supplying is never completely unrewarded.
- `Slope1` is the gentle pre-kink gradient. It rises smoothly with <Term id="utilisation">utilisation</Term> while the pool is healthy.
- `Slope2` is the cliff. It is deliberately steep because it is a liquidity defence, not a pricing strategy — it exists to force repayment fast.

Depositor yield is then derived from what borrowers actually pay, minus the protocol's cut:

`SupplyAPR = U × R_borrow × (1 - ReserveFactor)`

That last line explains why depositor yield rises with utilisation. The pool only earns interest on the fraction that is borrowed (`U`), and the reserve factor skims a slice for the protocol. Higher utilisation means more of your deposit is out working — and, past the kink, working at a dramatically higher rate.

questions.prompt: Why do DeFi lending protocols add a steep 'kink' to the interest rate curve above roughly 80% utilisation?
options: To maximise founder profits on every loan issued
Because Solana gas fees scale directly with pool utilisation
To automatically trigger liquidations of every open borrower
To force borrowers to repay and attract new deposits, so the pool is never drained empty
questions.explainRight: The kink is a liquidity defence, not a profit scheme. Past ~80% the curve spikes, which pressures borrowers to repay and tempts new depositors with a high <Term id="apy">APY</Term>. That two-sided push keeps the pool solvent.
questions.explainWrong: It is not about founder profits or gas fees, and it does not liquidate healthy borrowers. It is a self-correcting safety valve: steep rates above the kink refill the <Term id="liquidity_pool">pool</Term> before depositors are left unable to withdraw.

questions.prompt: A pool has $1,000,000 in USDC deposits and $400,000 in active borrows. What is the pool's utilisation rate?
questions.explainRight: Borrows over deposits: $400,000 / $1,000,000 = 40%. Comfortably below the kink, so borrowing here is still cheap and depositor yield is modest and safe.
questions.explainWrong: Do the division first. Utilisation cannot exceed 100% because you cannot borrow more than has been deposited, and 25% would imply only $250,000 borrowed.

questions.prompt: If utilisation is 25% and borrowers are paying 10% APR, roughly what supply APR can depositors expect before the reserve factor?
options: About 2.5%, because only the borrowed 25% of deposits is earning interest while the rest sits idle
About 10%, because every depositor earns the full borrow rate regardless of utilisation
About 40%, because the idle 75% is also lent out and earning
About 0%, because supply APY is independent of utilisation
questions.explainRight: Supply APR is roughly `U × R_borrow`, so 0.25 × 10% ≈ 2.5%. Only the borrowed portion generates interest, so low utilisation automatically produces lower depositor yield.
questions.explainWrong: Depositors never earn the full borrow rate, because idle deposits are not lent out. The right approximation is `U × R_borrow` ≈ 2.5%. Supply yield is deeply dependent on <Term id="utilisation">utilisation</Term>.

questions.prompt: Suppose utilisation climbs from 60% to 92% in a pool with an 80% kink. What happens to the borrow rate, and why?
options: It stays flat, because the base rate floors the curve at every level
It falls, because more borrowers spread the cost across the pool
It jumps sharply, because the pool has crossed the kink and the steep Slope2 now applies
It is unaffected until utilisation hits exactly 100%
questions.explainRight: Below 80% the rate follows Slope1, but 92% is past the kink so Slope2 applies and the <Term id="apr">APR</Term> shoots up. That jump is the point: it makes borrowing painful and depositing lucrative exactly when the pool needs help.
questions.explainWrong: The rate does not stay flat, fall, or wait for 100%. Crossing the kink switches the formula to the much steeper segment. The curve prices the last drops of liquidity very expensively on purpose.

questions.prompt: Two depositors supply identical amounts. Pool A runs at 20% utilisation and Pool B at 85%. Assuming similar base rates, why does Pool B pay much more?
options: Higher utilisation means more of every deposit is lent out, and being past the kink applies a dramatically higher interest rate to that borrowed capital
Pool B pays more because it charges depositors a fee to withdraw their money
Pool B mints extra reward tokens to inflate its advertised yield
Pool A pays more, since idle liquidity is safer and therefore yields more
questions.explainRight: Two effects stack. A larger share of deposits (85% vs 20%) is actively earning, and being past the kink means that borrowed capital is charged a much higher rate. More capital working, at a richer rate.
questions.explainWrong: Pool B does not charge withdrawal fees or mint fake rewards, and idle liquidity does not drive yield. The explanation is combination: more of the deposit is lent out *and* the kink raises the borrow <Term id="apr">APR</Term>.

questions.prompt: A whale deposits a huge amount of USDC into a pool sitting at 90% utilisation. All else equal, what is the most likely near-term effect?
options: Utilisation stays at 90% and the new deposit earns the old, elevated rate
The whale's deposit instantly pushes the pool past the kink toward 100%
Deposits do not affect utilisation, so nothing changes
Utilisation falls (more deposits, same borrows), which lowers the borrow rate and the whale's own yield - rewarding early exit for the existing lenders
questions.explainRight: Utilisation is borrows over deposits, so a large deposit raises the denominator and pushes U down. Coming back below the kink collapses the borrow rate — and with it the very yield the whale came for. The premium erases itself.
questions.explainWrong: Adding deposits cannot push utilisation toward 100%; it moves it the other way. The subtle lesson is that a high yield at a crunch is a signal to supply liquidity, and supplying it is precisely what removes the premium.

questions.prompt: Borrow demand suddenly surges, pushing a healthy pool from 50% to 95% utilisation. Which description best captures how the protocol self-heals?
options: Borrowers pay a fixed rate, so the pool relies on an administrator to add liquidity manually
The kinked rate spikes borrowing costs, forcing repayment, while boosting supply APY, attracting fresh deposits - pulling utilisation back below the kink with no manager involved
The protocol pauses all withdrawals until utilisation returns to 50%
High utilisation automatically liquidates every borrower to refill the pool
questions.explainRight: The kink works both sides at once. Borrowers face punishing rates that make repaying rational, and depositors see a huge <Term id="apy">APY</Term> that pulls in new capital. Borrows fall and deposits rise, so utilisation retreats below the kink on its own.
questions.explainWrong: There is no administrator, no withdrawal freeze, and no blanket liquidation of healthy loans. The curve heals itself by pricing the crunch: high borrow cost drives repayment while high supply yield attracts deposits.
